chapterNote: The psalm of the two books — the book of the world and the book of the Word, C. S. Lewis's candidate for the greatest poem in the Psalter. The first stanza reads creation: the heavens keep recounting the glory of God in a wordless speech that reaches every language, day pouring testimony to day, night handing knowledge to night, with the sun as chief witness — a bridegroom striding from his canopy, a champion rejoicing to run, and nothing hidden from his heat. Then at verse 7 the psalm pivots from El, the God of power the skies proclaim, to YHWH, the covenant LORD — named seven times — because the sun can show His glory but only the torah can restore a soul. Six titles of Scripture, six perfections, six effects: reviving the soul, making wise the simple, rejoicing the heart, enlightening the eyes, enduring forever, righteous altogether — worth more than much fine gold, sweeter than the honeycomb's dripping. And the third movement turns both books on the reader: the Word that warns exposes errors no self-scan can find, so the psalm ends in prayer — cleanse me from hidden faults, hold me back from presumptuous sins, and let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in Your sight, O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer.

1.text: For the choir director. A psalm of David. The heavens keep recounting the glory of God, and the expanse above declares the work of His hands.
1.amp: To the chief Musician [natsach], A Psalm [mizmor] of David. The heavens [shamayim] declare [saphar — recount, tally out] the glory [kabod] of God [El]; and the firmament [raqia — the expanse] shows [nagad] His handywork [maaseh yad — the work of His hands].
1.notes: saphar (H5608) is the counting-and-recounting verb: the skies keep books on the kabod (H3519) of El (H410), entry after entry. The raqia (H7549) is Genesis 1's own word for the expanse — creation reciting its Maker's resume without pause.

2.text: Day after day pours out speech like a bubbling spring, and night after night breathes out knowledge.
2.amp: Day [yom] unto day utters [naba — bubbles up, pours forth] speech [omer], and night [layil] unto night shows [chavah — declares, breathes out] knowledge [daat].
2.notes: naba (H5042) is a spring gushing: the testimony is under pressure, not squeezed out. Each yom hands the omer (H562) to the next, each layil passes daat (H1847) down the relay — an unbroken chain of witness running since the fourth day of creation.

3.text: There is no speech, there are no words; their voice goes unheard —
3.amp: There is no speech [omer] nor language [dabar], where their voice [qol] is not heard ['without these their voice is heard', the KJV margin].
3.notes: The paradox both readings preserve: the heavens' qol (H6963) is wordless — no omer, no dabar — and yet no tribe on earth is out of its range. Glory speaks the one language that needs no translation.

4.text: and yet their measuring line has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In the heavens He has pitched a tent for the sun,
4.amp: Their line ['rule, direction', qav, the KJV margin — the measuring line] is gone out [yatsa] through all the earth [eretz], and their words [millah] to the end [qatseh] of the world [tebel]. In them has He set [sum] a tabernacle [ohel — a tent] for the sun [shemesh],
4.notes: The qav (H6957) is a surveyor's line: the skies' message has staked its claim over every acre of the tebel (H8398). Paul quotes this verse for the gospel's own reach (cf. Romans 10:18). And within that witness, one ohel (H168) — the sun quartered in the sky like a champion in his tent.

5.text: and he comes out like a bridegroom leaving his wedding canopy; he rejoices like a mighty champion to run his course.
5.amp: Which is as a bridegroom [chathan] coming out [yatsa] of his chamber [chuppah — the wedding canopy], and rejoices [sus] as a strong man [gibbor — a champion] to run [ruts] a race [orach — his appointed course].
5.notes: Two similes for sunrise: the chathan (H2860) stepping radiant from the chuppah (H2646), joy and glory at once — and the gibbor (H1368) at the starting line, strength that delights in the distance. Dawn as wedding and footrace both.

6.text: His rising is from one end of the heavens, and his circuit runs to their farthest edge, and nothing is hidden from his heat.
6.amp: His going forth [motsa] is from the end [qatseh] of the heaven [shamayim], and his circuit [tequphah] unto the ends of it: and there is nothing hid [satar] from the heat [chammah] thereof.
6.notes: The tequphah (H8622) is the full circuit, horizon to horizon, and satar (H5641) the hiding-verb: nothing escapes the sun's heat — a line that quietly preps the psalm's turn, for neither does anything hide from the Word (cf. Hebrews 4:12-13).

7.text: The law of the LORD is perfect, restoring the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure and trustworthy, making wise the simple.
7.amp: The law [torah — instruction, teaching] of the LORD [YHWH] is perfect [tamim — complete, without defect], converting ['restoring', shub, the KJV margin] the soul [nephesh]: the testimony [eduth] of the LORD is sure [aman — firm, dependable], making wise [chakam] the simple [peti — the open, naive one].
7.notes: The pivot: El of the skies becomes YHWH (H3068) of the covenant, seven times in the stanza. torah (H8451) is teaching wider than statute, tamim (H8549) whole without defect — and its first effect is shub (H7725), bringing the nephesh back, the very verb of repentance. The peti (H6612), the wide-open simple one, walks out chakam.

8.text: The precepts of the LORD are right, making the heart rejoice; the commandment of the LORD is pure and clear, giving light to the eyes.
8.amp: The statutes [piqqud — precepts] of the LORD [YHWH] are right [yashar — straight], rejoicing [samach] the heart [leb]: the commandment [mitsvah] of the LORD is pure [bar — clear, radiant], enlightening [or — giving light to] the eyes [ayin].
8.notes: yashar (H3477), straight — precepts that run true like a well-cut road, and the straight road gladdens the leb that walks it. bar (H1249) is clarity like polished glass: the mitsvah (H4687) does for the ayin (H5869) what the sun of verse 6 does for the world.

9.text: The fear of the LORD is clean, standing firm forever; the judgments of the LORD are truth, and righteous through and through.
9.amp: The fear [yirah] of the LORD [YHWH] is clean [tahor], enduring [amad — standing firm] for ever [ad]: the judgments [mishpat] of the LORD are true ['truth', emeth, the KJV margin] and righteous [tsadaq] altogether [yachad].
9.notes: yirah (H3374) here stands for the Word that teaches it — reverence as Scripture's distilled effect, tahor (H2889) without a particle of corruption, amad (H5975) while empires rotate. His mishpatim are emeth (H571) — not merely true but truth itself — and tsadaq yachad, righteous as one seamless whole.

10.text: They are more to be desired than gold, than heaps of the finest gold; they are sweeter than honey, than the dripping of the honeycombs.
10.amp: More to be desired [chamad] are they than gold [zahab], yea, than much [rav] fine gold [paz]: sweeter [mathoq] also than honey [debash] and the honeycomb ['the dropping of honeycombs', nopheth, the KJV margin].
10.notes: Two appetites, wealth and sweetness, both outbid: paz (H6337) is gold refined to its purest, and nopheth (H5317) the honey that drips free of the comb untouched — the finest of the finest in each column, and the Word above both. chamad (H2530) is strong desire: the psalmist wants Scripture the way misers want gold.

11.text: By them, moreover, Your servant is warned and illumined, and the keeping of them carries great reward.
11.amp: Moreover by them is Your servant [ebed] warned [zahar — warned, made to shine]: and in keeping [shamar] of them there is great [rav] reward [eqev — consequence, what follows at the heel].
11.notes: zahar (H2094) carries both warning and shining — the Word alerts and illuminates in one act. eqev (H6118) is literally the heel: the reward is not payment appended to obedience but what follows in obedience's own footsteps — the keeping itself already walking in the good.

12.text: Who can discern his own wanderings? Declare me clean from the faults hidden even from me.
12.amp: Who can understand [bin — discern] his errors [shegiah — wanderings, strayings]? cleanse [naqah — acquit, declare clean] You me from secret [satar — hidden] faults.
12.notes: The two books close on the reader: under the Word's light the honest answer to 'who can bin (H995) his own strayings?' is no one. The satar-faults are hidden from the sinner himself, not merely from others — so the plea is naqah (H5352), the acquittal only God can pronounce.

13.text: Hold Your servant back from presumptuous sins as well; do not let them rule over me. Then I will be blameless, and innocent of great transgression.
13.amp: Keep back [chasak — restrain, withhold] Your servant [ebed] also from presumptuous [zed — proud, insolent] sins; let them not have dominion [mashal] over me: then shall I be upright [tamam — complete, blameless], and I shall be innocent [naqah] from the great ['much', rav, the KJV margin] transgression [pesha].
13.notes: The second sin-class: zedim (H2086), the high-handed, eyes-open sins — and the prayer knows they campaign for mashal (H4910), dominion, the ruling seat (cf. Genesis 4:7). chasak (H2820) asks God's restraining hand in advance; grace guards the gate, not just the cleanup.

14.text: May the words of my mouth and the murmured meditation of my heart find acceptance in Your sight, O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer.
14.amp: Let the words [emer] of my mouth [peh], and the meditation [higgayon — the murmuring, the inner music] of my heart [leb], be acceptable [ratson — delightful, well-pleasing] in Your sight [panim], O LORD [YHWH], my strength ['my rock', tsur, the KJV margin], and my redeemer [gaal — my Kinsman-Redeemer].
14.notes: The psalm that began with the heavens' speech ends asking that one man's speech join the choir: emer of the peh and higgayon (H1902) of the leb offered as ratson (H7522), an acceptable sacrifice. The closing titles pair granite and kinship — tsur (H6697), the Rock, and goel (H1350), the Redeemer who buys back His own; the prayer every preacher has borrowed since.
